items.title: Clicks bought with 90 pence
items.ask: An advertiser spends 90 pence on Google clicks one day in February, assuming an FX rate of 1.60 cents to 1 pence. How many clicks did he get? Options: 7, 8, 9, 10, 11.
items.how: 90 pence × 1.60 = 144 cents. The line chart shows a Google click costs 18 cents in February, so 144 ÷ 18 = 8 clicks.

items.title: Mounthill High: sport income if basketball switched to football
items.ask: What would be the percentage decrease in Mounthill High’s income from Sport extracurriculars if everyone switched from Basketball to Football? Options: 3.57%, 3.58%, 3.88%, 3.98%.
items.how: Mounthill sport income: Football 32 × $10 = 320, Basketball 15 × $12.50 = 187.50, Swimming 23 × $20 = 460, total 967.50. If the 15 basketball players switch to football they pay 15 × $10 = 150, a fall of 37.50. 37.50 ÷ 967.50 = 3.88%. (Counting only football and basketball as sport gives 7.4%, which is not an option, so swimming is included.)

items.title: Average weekly cost of an extra-curricular activity
items.ask: What is the average weekly cost of an extra-curricular activity? Options: $21.90, $21.92, $22.90, $22.92.
items.how: The average of the six activity prices: (32 + 10 + 12.50 + 38 + 25 + 20) ÷ 6 = 137.50 ÷ 6 = $22.92. Weighting by the number of participants would give about $20.63, which is not an option.

items.title: Cosmetics+: fall in in-store sales
items.ask: What was the percentage decrease in the amount on in-store sales from 2022 to 2023 for Cosmetics+? Options: 23.18%, 23.28%, 23.38%, 23.48%.
items.how: The chart label ‘COMETIC’ is read as Cosmetics+. Its in-store sales fell from 15.1 in 2022 to 11.6 in 2023: (15.1 − 11.6) ÷ 15.1 = 3.5 ÷ 15.1 = 23.18%.

items.title: Google (April) against Facebook and Yahoo (February)
items.ask: What was the ratio of the cost of a Google click in April compared to the cost of a Facebook and Yahoo click in February? Options: 1 : 0.90, 1 : 1.11, 1 : 1.27, 1 : 1.29, 1 : 3.00.
items.how: Google in April = 18 cents. Facebook (14) plus Yahoo (6) in February = 20 cents. 18 : 20 = 1 : 1.11. (14 : 18 would give 1 : 1.29 and 6 : 18 would give 1 : 3.00, which are the traps.)

items.title: Fund invested in Oil & Gas
items.ask: How much of the fund was invested in the Oil & Gas sector? Total value of fund $857m. Options: $119,980,000, $128,550,000, $248,530,000, $282,810,000.
items.how: The doughnut chart gives Oil & Gas 29%. 29% × $857m = 0.29 × 857 = $248.53m = $248,530,000. (14% would give $119.98m and 15% would give $128.55m, which are traps; 33% gives $282.81m.)

items.title: Japan: change in ships of 30,000 to 49,999 tonnes
items.ask: What is the percentage change in the number of ships between 30,000 and 49,999 tonnes in Japan from 2022 to 2023? Options: 26.95%, 31.63%, 32.85%, 35.90%.

items.title: Ratio of online to in-store sales, 4 stores, 2022
items.ask: What is the ratio of total online to in-store sales for these 4 stores in 2022? Options: 2.35:1, 2.45:1, 2.68:1, 2.73:1.
items.answer: No option matches exactly. Our working gives 2.78 : 1. The closest option is 2.73 : 1 (the last option). Check this one.
items.how: 2022 online: 58.5 + 28.5 + 45.6 + 38.4 = 171.0. 2022 in-store: 14.6 + 17.2 + 15.1 + 14.7 = 61.6. 171.0 ÷ 61.6 = 2.776, so 2.78 : 1. None of the four options is 2.78, so the printed values may be slightly misread or the question may have a different intended reading. The nearest is 2.73 : 1; the others are further away.

items.title: Largest in-store share of online sales, 2023
items.ask: Which seller had the largest in-store sales as a percentage of online sales in 2023? Options: Fashionista & Co, Home & About., Cosmetics+, SkinAlight.
items.how: In-store ÷ online for 2023. Fashionista & Co: 4.1 ÷ 69.3 = 5.9%. Home & About: 10.5 ÷ 54.8 = 19.2%. Cosmetics+: 11.6 ÷ 52.6 = 22.1%. SkinAlight: 4.9 ÷ 25.5 = 19.2%. Cosmetics+ is the highest. (The chart label ‘COMETIC’ is read as Cosmetics+.)

items.title: Average unemployed in London, Cardiff and Glasgow, 2019
items.ask: What was the average number of unemployed people in London, Cardiff and Glasgow in 2019? The chart is in thousands. Options: 3,333, 4,667, 5,667, 7,000.
items.how: The 2019 bars (dark blue) read London 6, Cardiff 4 and Glasgow 4, in thousands. (6 + 4 + 4) ÷ 3 = 14 ÷ 3 = 4.667 thousand = 4,667.

items.title: Mounthill High: average cost after a 15% rise in sports prices
items.ask: Mounthill High decides to increase the price of sports activities by 15%. What is their new average weekly cost of an extracurricular? Options: $23.98, $24.98, $25.98, $26.98.
items.how: Only the three sports rise by 15%: Football $10 × 1.15 = $11.50, Basketball $12.50 × 1.15 = $14.375, Swimming $20 × 1.15 = $23.00. The other three stay the same: Piano $32, Violin $38, Debating $25. Sum of the six prices = 11.50 + 14.375 + 23 + 32 + 38 + 25 = 143.875. Average = 143.875 ÷ 6 = $23.98. (Same simple average of the six prices as Item 3, where the old average was $22.92.)

items.title: Facebook click cost in July at the April-to-May rate
items.ask: If the cost of a Facebook click continued to decrease at the same rate as it did from April to May, how much will a click cost in July? Options: 5.28 cents, 10.61 cents, 2.43 cents, 10.56 cents, 8.58 cents.
items.how: Read the Facebook line (dark navy): April 16 cents, May 13 cents. The rate is a percentage fall: 13 ÷ 16 = 0.8125 a month, an 18.75% decrease. June = 13 × 0.8125 = 10.5625. July = 10.5625 × 0.8125 = 8.58 cents. (A flat fall of 3 cents a month would give 7 cents, which is not an option; 10.56 is the June value, a trap.)

items.title: Broken window: society does not benefit from repairing destroyed property
items.ask: Passage on the parable of the broken window (the glazier’s fallacy). Statement: ‘Society does not benefit from the cost of repairing destroyed property.’ Options: True, False, Cannot say.
items.how: The first sentence says the parable illustrates that ‘money spent due to destruction does not result in a benefit to society’. The passage then explains why the apparent job-creation benefit is an illusion. The statement restates the passage’s main point.

items.title: Birds: are ground-up and trees-down the only theories of flight?
items.ask: Passage on bird evolution and powered flight. Statement: ‘The “ground-up” and “trees-down” theories are the only theories explaining flight in birds.’ Options: True, False, Cannot say.
items.how: The passage says ‘Two theories of flight in birds are’ ground-up and trees-down. It does not say there are no others, and it only adds that the origin of powered flight is still debated. ‘Only’ cannot be confirmed or denied from the text.

items.title: Cats: do both stray and feral cats show hostility to humans?
items.ask: Passage on feral and stray cats. Statement: ‘Both stray and feral cats exhibit hostility when first encountering humans.’ Options: True, False, Cannot say.
items.how: The passage says ‘Unlike strays, feral cats initially show hostility towards humans, particularly upon first contact.’ So hostility on first contact is what separates feral cats from strays, and the statement that both do it contradicts the passage.

items.title: Cats: biodiversity and feral cat populations
items.ask: Same passage on feral and stray cats. Statement: ‘Biodiversity can be affected by feral cat populations.’ Options: True, False, Cannot say.
items.how: The passage says feral cats ‘may become invasive to ecosystems’, resulting in ‘a decline in biodiversity’, and have led to extinctions of some species. So biodiversity can be affected by them.

items.title: Internet access: what is the passage’s main argument?
items.ask: Passage on free internet access, bandwidth and tiered pricing. Statement: ‘The main argument in the passage is that internet users are not leaving enough bandwidth for 80% of the world’s population.’ Options: True, False, Cannot say.
items.answer: False (a judgement call: Cannot say is the other reading)
items.how: The passage opens with the question of free access for the 80% not online, then spends most of its length on the connected fifth’s demand outstripping bandwidth supply and on the debate over tiered pricing and net neutrality. It never argues that current users are taking bandwidth away from the unconnected, and it does not push one main argument at all, it lays out both sides. So the statement misdescribes the passage. If the real key says Cannot say, this is the item to double-check.

items.title: XSoft: did it withhold information about how long the project would take?
items.ask: Passage on a Private Finance Initiative project. Statement: ‘XSoft withheld information from the Department regarding how long the project would take.’ Options: True, False, Cannot say.
items.how: The passage says that in December 1997 XSoft ‘indicated they needed time to complete the project’, and that a more thorough estimate of timescales would have helped the Department. It never says XSoft hid anything: the problem described is an inadequate estimate, not concealment. So withholding can be neither confirmed nor ruled out.

items.title: Guns: invented because humans need to protect themselves?
items.ask: Passage on the gun’s effect on the world. Statement: ‘The gun was invented because the human race needs to protect themselves.’ Options: True, False, Cannot say.
items.how: The passage says many of the developments in gun design were brought about by man’s desire to protect himself. That is about later developments, not why the gun was first invented, so the statement about the invention itself goes beyond the text.

items.title: Guns: the reason our society is the way it is today?
items.ask: Same passage on the gun. Statement: ‘Guns are the reason our society is the way it is today.’ Options: True, False, Cannot say.
items.how: The passage only says the gun ‘helped in the development of society as we know it’ and had a profound effect on the world. Helping is not the same as being ‘the reason’, and the passage does not rule out other causes or say guns were the only one. If the real key says False, this is the item to double-check.

items.title: Social responsibility: can corporations influence the public’s quality of life?
items.ask: Passage on being socially responsible. Statement: ‘Corporations can influence the public’s quality of life.’ Options: True, False, Cannot say.
items.how: The passage says social responsibility directly affects quality of life (human rights, working conditions, the environment, corruption), and that the public have realised the influence of corporations, whose voluntary social responsibility initiatives have increased. So corporations can influence quality of life.

items.title: Food supplements: which statement is true?
items.ask: Passage on food supplements in the UK. Which one of the following statements is true, based on the paragraph alone? Options: Food supplements can aid weight loss; Half the UK population take multivitamin daily; Supplements are becoming increasingly popular; Supplements are not intended to replace a balanced diet.
items.answer: Supplements are not intended to replace a balanced diet (the last option)
items.how: The passage ends: ‘such supplements are not intended to replace a balanced diet’. The others fail: weight loss is never mentioned; ‘over half’ take any supplement and two thirds of those take multivitamins, so it is not half of the population on multivitamins; and nothing says supplements are becoming more popular.

items.title: Guns: did financial incentives play no part in their development?
items.ask: Passage on the gun’s effect on the world. Statement: ‘Financial incentives had no part to play in the development of the gun.’ Options: True, False, Cannot say.
items.how: The passage gives two drivers of gun design, man’s desire to protect himself and the challenge of inventing bigger and more accurate weapons. It never mentions money or financial incentives either way, so it cannot be said whether they played a part. (Do not read ‘these two reasons are given’ as ‘nothing else was involved’.)

items.title: Mismatched screenshot: social responsibility passage with the gun statement
items.ask: The screenshot shows the passage on being socially responsible (corporate social responsibility) but the statement under it is ‘Financial incentives had no part to play in the development of the gun.’ Options: True, False, Cannot say.
items.answer: Cannot say (the passage and the statement do not match: it looks like a form error)
items.how: This screenshot pairs the corporate social responsibility passage with the gun statement from Item 23. The passage never mentions guns or financial incentives, so against this text alone the answer is Cannot say. In the real test the statement was most likely meant for the gun passage (Item 23, also Cannot say), so either reading gives the same answer. Check it against the real form if you can.

items.title: XSoft: were the Department’s profits dependent on how long the project took?
items.ask: Passage on a Private Finance Initiative project. Statement: ‘The Department’s profits were dependent upon how long the project took.’ Options: True, False, Cannot say.
items.answer: True (the passage is slightly loose here, so double-check it)
items.how: The passage says the Department would have questioned starting the project ‘especially considering the implications of delay on the overall profitability for the venture’. So profitability depended on delay, and the length of the project affects it. The small gap is that the passage says the venture’s profitability, not the Department’s profits, so some keys may mark Cannot say.

items.title: Grid sequence: moving black, grey and circle squares
items.ask: Which of the boxes comes next in the sequence? Five 3×3 grids, then options A to E.
items.how: Three things move independently. The black square makes knight’s moves: top-left, middle-right, bottom-left, top-middle, bottom-right, so the next knight’s move (to a square not yet used) is middle-left. The circle steps one cell along the reading order each frame (cells 2, 3, 4, 5), so next is cell 6, middle-right. The grey square only appears in odd frames (bottom-right, top-right, top-left), so there is none in frame 6. That gives black middle-left, circle middle-right and no grey: option B.

items.title: Line and ball sequence: rotating ramp
items.ask: Which of the boxes comes next in the sequence? Five boxes each showing a ramp-like line with a ball, then options A to E.
items.answer: A (less certain: the pictures are small, so double-check)
items.how: The line turns 45° clockwise each frame: horizontal, then \ diagonal, vertical, / diagonal, horizontal, so frame 6 is the \ diagonal again, rotated a further 45° with the ball at the lower-right end. Options C and D simply repeat frames 1 and 2, and B is vertical, which leaves A (the \ diagonal with the ball at the lower-right end).

items.title: Rectangle sequence: black square, white square and circle in the corners
items.ask: Which of the boxes comes next in the sequence? Five rectangles with shapes in the corners, then options A to E.
items.how: Each shape moves clockwise round the corners. The black square goes top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left, top-left, so next is top-right. The white square goes bottom-left, top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left, so next is top-left. The circle shows only in even frames and moves two corners each time (bottom-left, then top-right), so next is bottom-left. Result: white top-left, black top-right, circle bottom-left: option E.

items.title: Shape sequence: top mark, body shape and arrow
items.ask: Which of the boxes comes next in the sequence? Five boxes with a shape on top of a larger shape (with or without an arrow), then options A to E.
items.how: Three rules. The top mark cycles in threes: black triangle, black bar, white oval, so next is the white oval. The body loses one side each frame: octagon, heptagon, hexagon, pentagon, rectangle, so next is a triangle. The arrow shows only in odd frames (right, left, right), so frame 6 has none. Oval on top of a triangle with no arrow: option B.

items.title: Arrow and rectangle sequence: colour, side and size
items.ask: Which of the boxes comes next in the sequence? Five boxes each with a chevron arrow and a rectangle, then options A to E.
items.how: The chevron alternates black at top-left and white at top-right, so frame 6 is white at top-right. The rectangle size repeats in threes: medium, large, small, medium, large, so frame 6 is small. White chevron at top-right with a small rectangle: option D.

items.title: Shape sequence: top shape, body shape and arrow
items.ask: Which of the boxes comes next in the sequence? Five boxes with a small shape on top of a larger shape (some with an arrow inside), then options A to E.
items.answer: E (less certain: the arrow rule is unclear, D is the alternative)
items.how: Three rules. The top shape cycles in threes: black pentagon, black hexagon, white square, so frame 6 has a white square on top (options D and E). The body loses a side each frame: octagon, heptagon, hexagon, pentagon, rectangle, so next is a triangle (both D and E). The arrow turns 90° clockwise each frame (right, down, left, up, right), so frame 6 points down: option E. The arrow is hidden in frames 2 and 4, which is the unclear part: if the arrow were to simply swap right and left, D (left) would be the answer. Double-check this one.

items.title: Rectangle sequence: black triangle, white triangle and circle with a cross
items.ask: Which of the boxes comes next in the sequence? Five rectangles with triangles and a crossed circle, then options A to E.
items.how: Each shape moves clockwise round the corners one step per frame. The black triangle goes top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left, top-left, so next is top-right. The white triangle goes bottom-left, top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left, so next is top-left. The crossed circle shows only in even frames and moves two corners each time (bottom-left, then top-right), so next is bottom-left. White triangle top-left, black triangle top-right, circle bottom-left: option E. Frame 5 is the same as frame 1, which confirms the cycle of four.

items.title: Dots above, crosses below: the missing box
items.ask: The boxes run in a sequence from left to right. Which box goes in the missing part of the sequence? Each box has dots in the top half and crosses in the bottom half; options A to D.
items.how: Count the dots in the top half: 5, 4, ?, 2, so the dots go down by one each box and the missing box has 3. Count the crosses in the bottom half: 1, 2, ?, 4, so the crosses go up by one and the missing box has 3. Option B has 3 dots (1 + 2) and 3 crosses (1 + 2). The others do not: A has 1 dot and 2 crosses, C has 1 dot and 3 crosses, D has 2 dots and 1 cross.

items.title: Grid pattern: arrows and shapes, the missing image
items.ask: Determine which image is missing from the pattern. Three rows of four pictures with a diagonal arrow and a shape, the last picture in the bottom row missing; options A to D.
items.how: In each row the fourth picture keeps only the shapes that sit next to a down-right arrow (↘) in the first three pictures, and has no arrow. Row 1: the down-right arrows go with the black circle and the white rectangle, and the fourth picture shows the rectangle and the circle. Row 2: only the white rectangle has a down-right arrow, and the fourth picture shows just the rectangle. Row 3: the down-right arrows go with the black hexagon and the white heart, so the missing picture shows a black hexagon and a white heart: option B.

items.title: Crosses sequence: square numbers
items.ask: The boxes run in a sequence from left to right. Which box goes in the missing part of the sequence? Boxes of crosses, with the second box missing; options A to D.
items.how: Count the crosses in the known boxes: 4, ?, 16, 25. These are the square numbers 2², 3², 4² and 5², so the missing box has 3² = 9 crosses. Option A has 9 crosses. B and C have 8 each, and D has 5.
